summary: Describes using GRE when IP is the delivery protocol, the payload protocol, or both. It also describes using IP addresses and autonomous system numbers as part of a GRE source route. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1702 describes Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE) when the Internet Protocol is involved: carrying GRE packets inside IP, carrying IP packets inside GRE, and carrying IP inside IP. It also defines GRE source routes built from IP addresses or from autonomous system numbers. The memo is companion material to the base GRE specification, RFC 1701.

questions: what ip protocol number does gre use
how does gre source routing work
subtitle: How GRE packets ride inside IP, how IP rides inside GRE, and how IP addresses and AS numbers form a GRE source route.

tldr.problem: RFC 1701 defined GRE as a way to wrap arbitrary packets in an arbitrary transport protocol, but it did not spell out what that means when the protocol involved is IP itself.
tldr.mechanism: This companion memo says GRE inside IP uses IP protocol type 47, IP inside GRE uses Protocol Type 0x800, and source route entries can hold IP addresses (Address Family 0x800) or autonomous system numbers (0xfffe).
tldr.outcome: It gives implementers the IPv4-specific rules for GRE. It is an Informational memo and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

today: RFC 1702 is an Informational memo. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 1701, the base GRE specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: An earlier memo, RFC 1701, described Generic Routing Encapsulation (GRE), a mechanism for encapsulating arbitrary packets within an arbitrary transport protocol. This companion memo describes the use of GRE with IP. It addresses three cases: IP as the delivery protocol, IP as the payload protocol, and the special case of IP as both delivery and payload. It also describes using IP addresses and autonomous system numbers as part of a GRE source route. The memo states that it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE wraps one packet inside another packet of a chosen transport protocol. This note covers the cases where internet packets are the wrapper, the wrapped item, or both.

sections.title: IP as Delivery Protocol and as Payload
sections.content:
GRE packets encapsulated within IP use IP protocol type 47. IP packets encapsulated within GRE carry a Protocol Type field of 0x800.

For the Address Family value 0x800, the Routing Information field consists of a list of IP addresses and indicates an IP source route. The first octet of the Routing Information field is an 8-bit integer offset from the start of the Source Route Entry (SRE), called the SRE Offset, which indicates the first octet of the next IP address. The SRE Length field is the total length of the IP address list in octets. For Address Family 0xfffe, the field consists of a list of autonomous system numbers and indicates an AS source route; the third octet is the SRE Offset, pointing at the first octet of the next AS number, and the SRE Length is the total length of the AS number list in octets.

When IP is encapsulated in IP, the TTL, TOS and IP security options MAY be copied from the payload packet into the same fields in the delivery packet. The payload packet's TTL MUST be decremented when the packet is decapsulated, to ensure that no packet lives forever.
sections.plainLanguage: GRE inside IP is IP protocol type 47. IP inside GRE is marked 0x800. An inner IP packet keeps its own lifetime counter, and that counter must be reduced when the outer packet is opened, so no packet survives indefinitely.

sections.title: IP and AS Source Routes
sections.content:
When a system processes an SRE with an Address Family indicating an IP source route, it MUST use the SRE Offset to determine the next destination IP address. If the next IP destination is this system, the SRE Offset is increased by four, the size of an IP address. If the SRE Offset equals the SRE Length, the Offset field in the GRE header is adjusted to point to the next SRE, if any. This repeats until the next IP destination is not this system or the whole SRE has been processed. If the source route is incomplete, the Strict Source Route bit is checked: for a strict route whose next IP destination is not an adjacent system, the packet MUST be dropped. Otherwise the system replaces the destination address in the delivery header with the address indicated by the offset and forwards the packet.

For an AS source route the same pattern applies with a two-octet step, the size of an autonomous system number. A system whose own autonomous system number matches the next one advances the offset by two and continues. If the source route is incomplete and the Strict Source Route bit is set while the next autonomous system is not an adjacent one, the packet should be dropped. Otherwise the system should use the autonomous system number indicated by the SRE Offset to replace the destination address in the delivery header and forward the packet. The exact mechanism for determining the next delivery destination address from an AS number is outside the scope of the memo.

The memo's Security Considerations section states only that security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: A GRE source route lists the hops a packet should follow, either as IP addresses or as autonomous system numbers. Each system checks the list, skips past its own entry, and forwards the packet. A strict route drops the packet if the next hop is not a direct neighbor.

fields.name: Address Family
fields.desc: 0x800 for an IP address list, 0xfffe for an AS number list.

fields.name: SRE Offset
fields.desc: Offset from the start of the SRE to the next address or number.

fields.name: SRE Length
fields.desc: Total length of the address or AS number list in octets.

references.text: Hanks, S., Li, T., Farinacci, D., and P. Traina, "Generic Routing Encapsulation", RFC 1701, October 1994.
